title: the Shiva Sahasranama (selections)
hook: Nilakantha, the blue-throated: the name Shiva earned by swallowing what nobody else would touch

segments.voice: Yesterday's selection from the Shiva Sahasranama was the Shiva Purana's frame story: Vishnu, a lotus at every name, and his eye when one went missing. What long thing did you finish with care? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-six.
screen: `A LOTUS AT EVERY NAME.` · `A NAME WITH A SCAR.`

segments.voice: In paintings and posters of Shiva, there's a detail that's easy to miss. Look at his throat. It's blue. Not his whole body, though he's often painted pale or ash-gray or blue all over. The throat, specifically, carries a darker stain, like a bruise. Some of his names describe how he looks or what he rules. This one remembers something he did, and it marks the place on his body where it happened. Today's selection from the Shiva Sahasranama is Nilakantha, the blue-throated one.
screen: `LOOK AT HIS THROAT.` → `A NAME THAT REMEMBERS.` → `NILAKANTHA.`

segments.voice: Nila is blue, a dark blue-black, and kantha is the throat. The story behind it is the churning of the ocean, told in the Mahabharata and in the Puranas. The gods and the demons want amrita, the nectar of immortality, and it lies at the bottom of the ocean of milk. So they make a churn out of a mountain, use the great serpent as the rope, and pull, the gods at one end and the demons at the other. Wonderful things rise out of the waves as they churn. But something terrible rises too: a poison, halahala, so strong it begins to burn the worlds. Nobody wants it. The gods and the demons both turn to Shiva. And Shiva drinks it. Here the tellings add a tender detail. In some, Parvati, his wife, puts her hand to his throat so the poison won't go down any further. In others his own power holds it there. Either way, the poison stops at the throat, and it stains it blue. He keeps the world safe by keeping the poison where it can't destroy him or anyone else. So the name is a scar, worn openly. It doesn't say Shiva is untouched by poison. It says he held it. Some readers reach for this story when someone in a family, or a workplace, takes in a hard thing so it doesn't spread: the bad news, the angry call, the blame. Not swallowing it so it eats you from inside. Not spitting it back at the room. Holding it at the throat, and letting it stop there.
screen: `NILA, KANTHA: BLUE, THROAT.` · `THE CHURNING OF THE OCEAN.` · `SHIVA DRINKS THE POISON.` · `HELD AT THE THROAT, NOT SWALLOWED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring your attention to the throat. Sit, and swallow once, and notice where that happens. Let the breath move through the throat slowly, cool on the way in, warm on the way out. Now let one hard thing from this week come to mind: a sharp word you heard, or one you almost said. Don't push it down into the belly. Don't send it out of the mouth. Just let it rest at the throat for a breath or two, and feel it lose some of its heat. If you pray, you can say Nilakantha softly. The bell holds the time.
The Shiva Sahasranama. Today's name from it: Nilakantha, the blue-throated, who drank the poison from the churning ocean and held it at his throat.

Your line: the Shiva Sahasranama, in selections. Today, when a complaint or a piece of bad news reaches you, let it stop with you instead of passing it down the line. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Hindus tell the churning of the ocean in the Mahabharata and the Puranas, and devotees honor Shiva as Nilakantha, the blue-throated one, in hymns, images and temples bearing that name.

fork.setup: a poison rises from the ocean and starts to burn the worlds. the gods and demons turn to you, Shiva. what do you do?
options: throw it back into the sea.
drink it, and hold it at your throat.
tell them to fix their own mess.
fork.reveal: Shiva drinks the halahala. it stops at his throat and stains it blue, so he's called Nilakantha.

original.note: Sanskrit: Nilakantha, blue (nila) throat (kantha); Shiva after drinking the poison.

trapdoor: what you thought: Shiva is painted blue because blue is a holy color.
what it means: the blue throat is a scar from the poison he held to save the worlds.
what a scholar hears: the churning of the ocean of milk in the Mahabharata and Puranas, where the halahala poison gives Shiva the name Nilakantha.
